overview: Aotearoa New Zealand's history includes Māori settlement and innovation, colonization, campaigns for rights and the development of a modern state. Archaeological remains, carved buildings, petitions and homes reveal both achievement and unequal power. Constitutional independence developed through several steps; no single change of title explains the whole story.

periods.title: Dominion status and expanding autonomy
periods.summary: New Zealand adopted the title of dominion in 1907 while retaining close imperial ties. Constitutional autonomy expanded, but the country did not adopt the Statute of Westminster until 1947. Dominion status alone was not a complete break with Britain.

periods.title: Constitutional independence and continuing change
periods.summary: Adoption of the Statute of Westminster in 1947 affirmed wider legislative autonomy. The Constitution Act 1986 removed the remaining provision for Britain to legislate for New Zealand. These steps concern the modern state and are distinct from Māori histories and authority.

items.text: Research places Polynesian settlement of Aotearoa around 1300 CE. At Wairau Bar, evidence extends beyond burials to structures, cooking and stone-tool production. A large stone-lined oven and animal remains help reconstruct village activities during an early phase of Māori history.

The 2009 Wairau Bar research followed an invitation from Rangitāne mana whenua alongside the return and reburial of ancestral remains. Geophysical survey and excavation examined the wider settlement. The history of research therefore includes community authority and relationships, as well as what was found.

Raharuhi Rukupō began Te Hau-ki-Tūranga at Manutūkē in 1842 as a memorial to his elder brother. Expert carvers worked on its posts and structure. Rukupō learned inherited techniques and later adopted steel tools, showing innovation within an established artistic tradition.

The government had Te Hau-ki-Tūranga dismantled and removed in 1867 during the confiscation of Tūranga lands. Payments went to people later found not to be its owners. Its subsequent museum display must therefore be understood alongside the coercive circumstances of removal.

Te Tiriti o Waitangi and its English counterpart were signed in 1840, but their terms concerning authority differ. The Māori text uses kāwanatanga and guarantees tino rangatiratanga; the English text speaks of sovereignty. Those differences matter when interpreting what rangatira and the Crown understood they had agreed.

The surviving 1893 women's suffrage petition consists of sheets gathered across the country and pasted into a roll by Kate Sheppard. Its physical form records collective organizing through meetings, travel and persuasion, not only the actions of a single prominent campaigner.

The Electoral Act signed on 19 September 1893 gave women the parliamentary vote. Earlier petition campaigns had failed in the Legislative Council. The successful reform followed repeated organizing and political struggle rather than a sudden, unopposed concession.

The sailing ship Dunedin carried a successful frozen-meat shipment to Britain in 1882 using a coal-powered freezing plant. Meat from Totara Estate moved by rail to Port Chalmers before freezing aboard. The achievement depended on an organized chain of workers, transport and temperature control.

Refrigerated shipping needed marketing and insurance arrangements as well as machinery. Its growth supported meat and dairy exports and reshaped farming. This was an application and organization of refrigeration technology, not evidence that refrigeration itself was invented in New Zealand.

The house at 12 Fife Lane in Miramar opened in 1937 as the first of the Labour government's new state houses. Photographs of the opening made it a public symbol, but for David and Mary McGregor it was also a family home entered by crowds of visitors.

David McGregor worked as a tram driver. The family initially paid rent and later bought the house under a changed policy. Following one household links a national housing program with wages, tenure and the practical wish for a secure place to live.

Born and educated in New Zealand, Ernest Rutherford developed the nuclear model of the atom in 1911 while working in Manchester. Scattering experiments involving Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden helped establish a small central nucleus. His achievement belongs to an international research setting, not an isolated national invention.

New Zealand adopted the Statute of Westminster on 25 November 1947. The Constitution Act 1986 later removed the remaining provision for British legislation. These milestones show a gradual change in the state's relationship with Britain, rather than an independence date inferred from a map boundary.

ending.text: New Zealand continues as a state. Its relationship with Britain changed through dominion status, the 1947 statute adoption and later constitutional reform. Māori communities and authority have their own continuing histories, including the unresolved consequences of colonial land loss and differing understandings of Te Tiriti.
